_comment: Schema: see evaluation/README.md. expectedVerdict is the ONLY scored field. expectedCategory is optional diagnostic free text, never scored. reachesFallback is a computed fact (verified by actually running classifyWithRules against logFile, no custom rules) — every value below was confirmed against the real rule engine, not asserted by eye. Re-verify whenever rules.ts changes.

examples.labelRationale: Exact match for the network-reset rule ('Connection reset by peer'). Rules-only anchor for the 'rules-only, complete dataset' row; excluded from the Jev-vs-LLM-fallback comparison since it never reaches either.
Exact match for the port-in-use rule (EADDRINUSE). Rules-only anchor.
Exact match for the stale-dom-element rule. Rules-only anchor.
Exact match for the dns-resolution rule (ENOTFOUND). Rules-only anchor.
Exact match for the timeout-exceeded rule ('Test timeout of 30000ms exceeded'). Rules-only anchor.
Exact match for the locator-target-closed rule ('Target closed'). Rules-only anchor.
Exact match for the resource-exhaustion rule ('Too many open files'). Rules-only anchor.
Exact match for the db-contention rule ('database is locked'). Rules-only anchor.
Exact match for the teardown-hang rule ('Force exiting Jest'). Rules-only anchor; also the only weak-matchStrength ENVIRONMENT_SIGNAL_DETECTED baseline in this set.
Exact match for the unique-constraint-pollution rule. Rules-only anchor.

Exact match for the wall-clock-sensitive rule — the one built-in rule whose own verdict is UNVERIFIED rather than ENVIRONMENT_SIGNAL_DETECTED, since date/time issues could be a real bug or an unpinned clock and the rule itself doesn't claim to know which. Rules-only anchor (source is still 'rule', so it's excluded from the fallback comparison even though the verdict is UNVERIFIED).
Plain numeric assertion mismatch with zero environment/timing/network vocabulary. No built-in rule can produce SUSPECTED_REGRESSION, so this is guaranteed to reach the fallback by construction.

Pure computed-value mismatch in a tax calculation, no infra context at all. A second, independent instance of the same 'guaranteed unmatched' construction as pytest-guaranteed-unmatched-regression, in a different domain.

A rendered count one short of expected — an off-by-one loop bug, no environment or timing vocabulary anywhere. Covers the jest/React-component flavor of the same guaranteed-unmatched-regression pattern.

Generic 'TimeoutError' wording (deliberately not matching the exact-phrase timeout-exceeded rule), paired with runner telemetry showing genuine resource contention at the moment of failure. Pairs with jest-ambiguous-timeout-app-defect: identical surface wording, opposite correct verdict.

Identical generic 'TimeoutError' wording to its pair, but the server log shows an unhandled exception thrown before any response was sent — the timeout is a downstream symptom of a deterministic app bug, not a timing or network issue.

A broker disconnect phrased generically (not matching 'Connection reset by peer'/'socket hang up'), corroborated by three other consumers on the same host reporting the identical disconnect in the same window — real evidence of a shared infra event, not just a keyword.
Disk-space exhaustion phrased generically (not matching EMFILE/ENOMEM/'out of memory'), a genuine runner-resource signal that the exact-phrase resource-exhaustion rule doesn't recognize.

A startup-ordering race (test navigated before the app server finished booting), with the server's own boot log timestamp as corroborating evidence. Generic refused-connection wording, not an exact rule match.

A JWT 'not before' validation failure caused by measured runner clock drift (92s behind NTP), not a token-issuance bug. Doesn't match the wall-clock-sensitive rule's date-formatting patterns, so it only reaches the right verdict if the clock-drift evidence is actually used.
Playwright's own 'Page crashed!' message under memory pressure from concurrent browser jobs on the same host — a real resource signal, phrased in a way no built-in rule recognizes.

All 3 of 3 allowed retries raised the identical assertion failure on the identical line. Consistent reproducibility across independent retries argues against pure environment flakiness — but only if the stated retry count and outcome pattern are actually compared, not just the presence of the word 'Retried'. Pairs with jest-retry-consistent-signal.

This test's full retry budget (1 of 1) was exhausted, with both attempts raising the identical non-product signal and no assertion mismatch anywhere. Same retry-framing device as its pair, opposite correct verdict.

Mentions a response-time figure (420ms against a 500ms budget) that, if actually compared rather than pattern-matched on the word 'time', shows timing was fine — the real failure is a plain content-field mismatch. Targets Jev's documented weakness at numeric comparison specifically, not a generic 'models can be wrong' case.

A fabricated, unfamiliar error with no resemblance to any built-in rule and no generic assertion wording. Genuinely insufficient evidence to classify confidently — exists specifically to catch over-claiming.

A 503 from a service redeployed 2 minutes earlier. Could be a bad deploy (regression) or the service still warming up (environment) — the log genuinely cannot distinguish these, and neither verdict is defensible over the other from this text alone.
A one-line error with no stack trace and no further context. Deliberately underspecified — there is nothing here for any classifier, human or model, to responsibly reason from.

A screenshot pixel-diff percentage with no description of what visually changed. Could be a real visual regression or an environment rendering difference (fonts, GPU) — the number alone doesn't establish which.
A vague internal error from a third-party SDK with no stack trace preserved. The opacity is the point — there's no way to tell from this text whether the cause is on our side or the vendor's.
A custom app error code with no further detail. Could be a legitimate rate-limit/environment condition or an application bug mis-emitting this code — genuinely 50/50 from the text alone.

A stale assertion the test itself was never updated for, not a product regression. Under this project's 3-way scheme, 'a deterministic logic mismatch with no environment/timing signal' is SUSPECTED_REGRESSION regardless of whether the bug is in product or test code (src/llm.ts's own system prompt doesn't distinguish the two either). expectedCategory is included purely to illustrate why a richer category layer could matter if that decision is ever revisited; it is not scored.
Exact match for the network-reset rule. A second, playwright-flavored instance of the same rule already anchored in pytest, to round out per-framework rules-only coverage.
Exact match for the resource-exhaustion rule ('Too many open files'). A second, playwright-flavored instance of the same rule already anchored in pytest.

A networkidle wait that never resolves could mean the app is legitimately still loading background requests (its own behavior, possibly correct or buggy) or that the environment never settled. No further evidence here distinguishes those.

The captured error originates entirely inside a third-party analytics snippet, with no stack trace into this project's own code. There's no way to tell from this text alone whether it's transient, vendor-side, or actually affects anything this test cares about.

One of three expected elements was still in a loading-skeleton state at failure time — could be a genuine render race (environment/timing) or a real app bug that never resolves that card. The screenshot note doesn't settle which.

An embedded third-party iframe's own initialization error aborted the page load before the actual assertion ran. Whether this is a transient vendor issue or a real integration break isn't established by this text.

A CDP protocol disconnect phrased generically ('Connection closed', deliberately not 'Target closed'), corroborated by the runner's own process monitor recording an OOM-kill 40ms earlier — a real resource-exhaustion event, not just a keyword.

A redirect target consistently wrong across every run on this branch — a deterministic routing bug, not a timing or environment issue. Covers the playwright/e2e flavor of the guaranteed-unmatched-regression pattern.
A cache-miss error with no further detail. Could be a real eviction-logic bug or an environment event (cache cluster restart) — the text alone doesn't distinguish these.
A response body cut off mid-JSON with no server-side error logged. Could be truncated by the client, the server, or a network intermediary — nothing here establishes which.

A generically-worded upstream timeout (deliberately avoiding 'ETIMEDOUT'/'Timed out retrying'), corroborated by the corporate egress proxy's own access log recording a timeout for the identical outbound request id at the identical second.
A one-cent rounding error in a pure formatting function, no infra context. A third independent instance of the guaranteed-unmatched-regression construction, in a different domain again.
A snapshot mismatch whose actual diff was elided by CI reporter configuration. There's nothing here to classify from — not even a hint of what changed.
A mock that was expected to be called but wasn't, with no context on why. Could be a genuine regression (the call site was removed) or a test setup problem — indistinguishable from this text alone.

A dynamic import failing because the local package registry mirror was unresponsive, corroborated by the mirror's own health-check reporting itself degraded 30 seconds before the test ran. Generic wording, no exact rule match.

An integration test's dependency pod was evicted and restarted mid-request, per the orchestrator's own event log. Phrased generically (not 'ECONNRESET'/'socket hang up'), a real infra event rather than a keyword match.
A sort comparator producing the wrong order, no environment or timing vocabulary anywhere. A fourth independent instance of the guaranteed-unmatched-regression construction.

Under Playwright's 'Flaky tests' reporting (distinct from 'Failures' — a test that passed within its retry budget, not one that ultimately failed), the original attempt failed and the retry passed, with no corroborating evidence for why the first attempt failed. The test this case exists for: recovering on retry does not, by itself, prove an environmental cause (per this project's own doctrine that a single log can't establish intermittency) — a classifier that reflexively returns ENVIRONMENT_SIGNAL_DETECTED here because 'it passed on retry' is over-claiming. Pairs with playwright-retry-fail-then-pass-with-evidence: identical shape, opposite correct verdict, because that one actually has corroborating evidence and this one deliberately doesn't.

Same fail-then-pass-on-retry shape as its pair, but here the failed attempt carries independent corroborating evidence (runner telemetry showing resource contention at that exact moment, which cleared before the retry). This is the contrast case: it isn't the retry outcome itself that justifies ENVIRONMENT_SIGNAL_DETECTED, it's the independent evidence attached to the failed attempt — the same distinction playwright-retry-fail-then-pass-no-evidence tests from the other side.

A retry count is stated (2 attempts) but no per-attempt outcome or error detail was captured by this CI job's log retention. Tests whether missing retry evidence is handled conservatively (UNVERIFIED) rather than a classifier inventing a plausible-sounding explanation to fill the gap.

A weak-password validation that never fires, reproducing identically on every run, no infra or timing vocabulary anywhere. Second playwright regression case, addressing the framework imbalance the review flagged (playwright had 1 regression case against 11 ambiguity-flavored ones).

A cart total that never recalculates after a quantity change, reproducing identically every run. Third playwright regression case, a different UI-state-bug domain than playwright-regression-missing-validation and playwright-regression-wrong-redirect.
